description:
Somos estudiantes de Geología de la Facultad de Tecnología y Ciencias Aplicadas y queremos llevar la Puna catamarqueña hasta lo más alto.

Aportamos geología, mineralogía y trabajo de campo, y nos apasiona la astrobiología y los análogos marcianos ¡Sumate si querés ayudarnos a valorizar un patrimonio único! Buscamos apasionados por la programación, SIG/teledetección, diseño gráfico y comunicación. ¡No hace falta ser experto, solo ganas de explorar!
summary:
We developed an interactive web map and analysis framework that compares the Campo de Piedra Pómez, an ignimbrite field in Argentina’s Puna, with Mars’s Medusae Fossae Formation (MFF) as a terrestrial analog. Using ASTER satellite data processed in Google Earth Engine, we mapped spectral indices for minerals linked to past water and potentially habitable environments: carbonates, Mg-OH and Al-OH clays, ferric iron oxides and silica. These layers can be toggled over a satellite basemap, beside the USGS geologic map of Mars with a NASA Mars Trek background, a scale bar and a unit legend. The comparison is organized around three axes: mineralogy, geomorphology (wind-carved yardangs in both regions) and radiation, using natural radioactivity (potassium, thorium and uranium) as a complementary variable.

The project addresses the challenge by offering a low-cost way to evaluate Earth sites as analogs of Martian terrains. It supports the selection of zones for instrument testing, mobility trials and, eventually, bases or landing sites. It matters because remotely detecting water-related minerals and understanding surface processes and radiation are central to the search for life on Mars. Analog sites let us validate those methods before applying them to orbital data. Results are relative spectral domains that still require validation with X-ray diffraction and fieldwork.
details:
What it does and how it works

The project is a three-page interactive website that compares the Campo de Piedra Pómez (CDPP), an ignimbrite field in Argentina’s Puna, with the Medusae Fossae Formation (MFF) on Mars, a Martian deposit that looks like it was carved by wind in a similar way. Each page looks at the analog from a different angle.

Page 1: Mineralogy and geology.

  1. We selected a low-cloud ASTER L1T scene of the CDPP in Google Earth Engine and computed band-ratio indices for minerals that form through interaction with water: carbonates, Mg-OH and Al-OH minerals, ferric iron oxides and silica/quartz.
  2. The indices were combined into RGB composites, stretched channel by channel (2nd to 98th percentile) and exported as GeoTIFF files.
  3. The USGS Geologic Map of Mars (Tanaka et al., 2014) was recalibrated and reprojected to an equirectangular projection so that it sits on NASA Mars Trek background tiles. The MFF appears continuous across the 180° E line.
  4. Two linked maps are shown side by side. On the Earth map, the user toggles the spectral layers, adjusts their opacity and changes the basemap. On the Mars map, the user adjusts the geologic map’s opacity, jumps to the MFF, opens the unit legend and reads a scale bar calculated with Mars’s radius.

Page 2: Radiation. It compares both regions through natural radioactivity (potassium, thorium and uranium) using radiometric maps. These elements are tied to rock composition, so the page complements the geological analogy. It also frames radiation as an environmental factor for habitability and for preserving organic compounds on Mars, where the thin atmosphere and the lack of a strong global magnetic field expose the surface to more radiation than on Earth.

Page 3: Geomorphology. It compares the landforms of both regions, centered on yardangs: elongated ridges, deflation corridors and eroded surfaces carved by persistent wind in friable materials. The orientation of these forms records dominant wind directions. The page connects them to the study of wind erosion, sediment transport and dust storms on Mars.

Benefits

  • It runs in any browser, with no software to install, and can be hosted for free as a static site.
  • It is built entirely on open, public data.
  • It integrates three independent lines of evidence (mineralogy, geomorphology and radiation) into one navigable resource, instead of a single map.
  • It makes the Earth–Mars comparison visual and quantitative, with real scale.
  • It is easy to extend to other analog sites or other data layers.

Intended impact

  • To support the selection and prioritization of terrestrial analog sites for testing instruments, mobility and methods, and, in the longer term, for identifying zones of interest for bases or landing sites.
  • To show that remote-sensing methods for detecting water-related minerals can be validated on Earth before being applied to orbital data from Mars.
  • To strengthen planetary-analog research and outreach in Argentina’s Puna.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data and platforms: ASTER L1T (NASA/METI/AIST/USGS LP DAAC), Google Earth Engine, USGS Geologic Map of Mars, NASA Mars Trek WMTS tiles, Esri, OpenStreetMap and OpenTopoMap basemaps, and radiometric maps for the radiation page.
  • Languages and libraries: JavaScript (Earth Engine and web pages), HTML/CSS, Leaflet.js, Python (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow), and Node.js (docx) for the technical document.
  • Hardware: a standard personal computer and web browser; no special equipment.
  • Development support: an AI assistant (Claude) helped with code, data processing and documentation. Remove or adjust this line according to the event’s rules.

What makes it creative

  • It links spectral mineralogy to the search for water and habitable environments, using a terrestrial site as a testbed for Mars.
  • It combines three complementary views (minerals, landforms and radiation) of the same analog pair.
  • It brings two worlds into one interface, with a reprojection built so that a feature that straddles the map edge on Mars appears whole, and a scale bar based on Mars’s radius.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific rigor: the indices show relative spectral domains, not identified minerals or abundances. They require validation with X-ray diffraction and fieldwork.
  • Data limits: ASTER’s thermal bands have a 90 m effective resolution, and its SWIR bands are valid only for scenes before April 2008. We audited the index formulas, and one composite (Silica/Quartz/Carbonate) is flagged as provisional until its quartz channel is recomputed.
  • Scale and projection: we avoided Robinson’s distortion near the equator by reprojecting and by adding a scale bar.
  • Limits of the analogy: it is strong for landforms and rock type, but weak for atmosphere and radiation. A landform or a mineral alone is not evidence of water or life, and must be complemented with geological and environmental data.
